steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper introducing Gated SAEs, a modified sparse autoencoder architecture for dictionary learning in mechanistic interpretability. It should motivate the problem, explain what we changed and how we evaluated it, and end with a list of our contributions.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Mechanistic interpretability, linear representations, neurons
   - goal: explain how NNs produce outputs via learned algorithms executed in forward pass
   - many concept representations appear linear
   - finding set of all interpretable directions: highly non-trivial
   - interpreting neurons (= directions in standard basis) insufficient: many polysemantic, fire on range of seemingly unrelated concepts

2. Superposition hypothesis -> SAEs
   - mechanistic explanation for these observations
   - intermediate representation of dimension n; model encodes M\gg n concepts as linear directions
   - set of concepts + directions fixed across all inputs; on given input only sparse subset active
   - -> not much simultaneous interference between (non-orthogonal) concepts
   - motivated by this, recent work used sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to find sparse decompositions of activations in an overcomplete basis / dictionary

3. L1 penalty problem; Gated SAE
   - SAEs promising, but L1 penalty (prevailing training method, encourages sparsity) introduces biases -> hurts reconstruction accuracy
   - loss can be decreased by trading some reconstruction accuracy for lower L1
   - "baseline SAE" = existing methodology, defined in Section 2.1 - 2.2, borrows heavily from prior work
   - our modification: Gated SAE + accompanying loss function; partially overcomes limitations
   - key insight: separate affine transformations for (a) which dictionary elements to use, (b) estimating coefficients of active elements; sparsity penalty only on (a)
   - share subset of weights between them -> no big increase in parameter count / inference-time compute vs baseline SAE of equivalent width

4. Evaluation
   - models: one layer GELU activation language models, Pythia-2.8B, Gemma-7B
   - sites: MLP layer outputs, attention layer outputs, residual stream activations
   - result: Gated SAEs Pareto improvement over baseline at fixed training compute (Fig. 1) - sparser decompositions at any level of reconstruction fidelity
   - follow-up ablations/investigations on subset of models + sites

5. Contributions
   - Gated SAE: decouples detecting which features present from estimating magnitudes (Section 3.2)
   - Pareto improvement in sparsity vs reconstruction fidelity trade-off vs baseline (Section 4.1)
   - overcomes shrinkage problem (Section 4.2); beats other methods addressing it (Section 5.1)
   - small double-blind study: features comparably interpretable to baseline (Section 4.3)

Mechanistic interpretability research tries to explain how neural networks produce their outputs, in terms of the learned algorithms that are executed during a forward pass. A lot of work uses the fact that many concept representations seem to be linear. However finding the set of all the interpretable directions is a highly non-trivial problem. The classic approaches like interpreting neurons (i.e. directions in the standard basis) are not enough, since many neurons are polysemantic and they tend to activate for a range of different concepts that seem unrelated.

The superposition hypothesis gives a mechanistic explanation for these observations. The idea is that in an intermediate representation of dimension n, a model will encode M\gg n concepts as linear directions. The set of concepts and their directions is fixed across all inputs, but on any given input only a sparse subset of the concepts are active, which means there is not much simultaneous interference between these concepts (which are non-orthogonal). Motivated by the superposition hypothesis, recent work used sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to find sparse decompositions of the model activations in terms of an overcomplete basis, or dictionary.

SAEs look promising for this, but the L1 penalty that the prevailing training method uses to encourage sparsity also introduces biases, and these harm the accuracy of SAE reconstructions, because the loss can go down by trading off some reconstruction accuracy for lower L1. We call the existing training methodology the baseline SAE (defined fully in Section 2.1 - 2.2, borrows heavily from earlier work).

- share a subset of weights between the two -> parameter count and inference-time compute not significantly increased vs baseline SAE of equivalent width

- models: one layer GELU activation language models, Pythia-2.8B, Gemma-7B
- sites: MLP layer outputs, attention layer outputs, residual stream activations
- Gated SAEs = Pareto improvement over baseline SAEs at fixed training compute (Fig. 1); sparser decompositions at any desired reconstruction fidelity
- further ablations / investigations on a subset of models and sites

- Gated SAE, decouples detection of present features from magnitude estimation (Section 3.2)
- Pareto improves sparsity / reconstruction fidelity trade-off vs baseline (Section 4.1)

steps.text:
Mechanistic interpretability research tries to explain how neural networks produce their outputs, in terms of the learned algorithms that are executed during a forward pass [1,2]. A lot of work uses the fact that many concept representations seem to be linear [3,4,2,5]. However finding the set of all the interpretable directions is a highly non-trivial problem. The classic approaches like interpreting neurons (i.e. directions in the standard basis) are not enough, since many neurons are polysemantic and they tend to activate for a range of different concepts that seem unrelated [6,7,8].

The superposition hypothesis [8] gives a mechanistic explanation for these observations. The idea is that in an intermediate representation of dimension n, a model will encode M\gg n concepts as linear directions. The set of concepts and their directions is fixed across all inputs, but on any given input only a sparse subset of the concepts are active, which means there is not much simultaneous interference [4] between these concepts (which are non-orthogonal). Motivated by the superposition hypothesis, [9] and [10] recently used sparse autoencoders (SAEs; [11]) to find sparse decompositions of the model activations in terms of an overcomplete basis, or dictionary [12].

SAEs look promising for this, but the L1 penalty that the prevailing training method uses to encourage sparsity also introduces biases, and these harm the accuracy of SAE reconstructions, because the loss can go down by trading off some reconstruction accuracy for lower L1. We call the existing training methodology the baseline SAE, which is defined fully in Section 2.1 - 2.2 and which borrows heavily from [9]. In this paper we introduce a modification to the baseline SAE architecture, which we call a Gated SAE, and also an accompanying loss function, and this partially overcomes these limitations. The key insight is that we use separate affine transformations for (a) determining which dictionary elements to use in a reconstruction and (b) estimating the coefficients of the active elements, and we only apply the sparsity penalty to the first one. To avoid significantly increasing the parameter count and the inference-time compute of a Gated SAE compared to a baseline SAE of equivalent width, we share a subset of weights between the two transformations.

We evaluate Gated SAEs on several models, a one layer GELU activation language models [13], Pythia-2.8B [14] and Gemma-7B [15], and on several sites within the models, MLP layer outputs, attention layer outputs, and residual stream activations. Across all of these models and sites we find that Gated SAEs are a Pareto improvement over baseline SAEs when training compute is held fixed (Fig. 1), meaning they give sparser decompositions at any level of reconstruction fidelity that you want. We also do some follow up ablations and investigations on a subset of the models and sites, to understand better how Gated SAEs and baseline SAEs differ.

So the key contributions of this work are that we:

1. Introduce the Gated SAE, which is a modification to the standard SAE architecture that decouples detecting which features are present from estimating how big they are (Section 3.2);

2. Show that Gated SAEs Pareto improve the trade-off between sparsity and reconstruction fidelity compared to baseline SAEs (Section 4.1);

3. Confirm that Gated SAEs overcome the shrinkage problem (Section 4.2), and that they outperform other methods which also address this problem (Section 5.1);

4. Give evidence from a small double-blind study that Gated SAE features are about as interpretable as baseline SAE features (Section 4.3).

steps.text:
Mechanistic interpretability research aims to explain how neural networks produce outputs in terms of the learned algorithms executed during a forward pass [1,2]. Much work relies on the fact that many concept representations appear to be linear [3,4,2,5]. However, finding the set of all interpretable directions is a highly non-trivial problem. Classic approaches, like interpreting neurons (i.e. directions in the standard basis), are insufficient, as many neurons are polysemantic and tend to activate for a range of different, seemingly unrelated concepts [6,7,8].

The superposition hypothesis [8] offers a mechanistic explanation for these observations: in an intermediate representation of dimension n, a model will encode M\gg n concepts as linear directions, where the set of concepts and their directions is fixed across all inputs, but on a given input only a sparse subset of concepts is active, so that there is not much simultaneous interference [4] between these (non-orthogonal) concepts. Motivated by the superposition hypothesis, [9] and [10] recently used sparse autoencoders (SAEs; [11]) to find sparse decompositions of model activations in terms of an overcomplete basis, or dictionary [12].

Although SAEs show promise in this regard, the L1 penalty used in the prevailing training method to encourage sparsity also introduces biases that harm the accuracy of SAE reconstructions, since the loss can be decreased by trading off some reconstruction accuracy for lower L1. We refer to this existing training methodology as the baseline SAE, defined fully in Section 2.1 - 2.2, which borrows heavily from [9]. In this paper, we introduce a modification to the baseline SAE architecture – a Gated SAE – together with an accompanying loss function, which partially overcomes these limitations. Our key insight is to use separate affine transformations for (a) determining which dictionary elements to use in a reconstruction and (b) estimating the coefficients of active elements, and to apply the sparsity penalty only to the former. We share a subset of weights between these transformations to avoid significantly increasing the parameter count and inference-time compute of a Gated SAE compared to a baseline SAE of equivalent width.

We evaluate Gated SAEs on multiple models: a one layer GELU activation language models [13], Pythia-2.8B [14] and Gemma-7B [15], and on multiple sites within models: MLP layer outputs, attention layer outputs, and residual stream activations. Across these models and sites, we find Gated SAEs to be a Pareto improvement over baseline SAEs with training compute held fixed (Fig. 1): they yield sparser decompositions at any desired level of reconstruction fidelity. We also conduct further follow up ablations and investigations on a subset of these models and sites to better understand how Gated SAEs and baseline SAEs differ.

Overall, the key contributions of this work are that we:

1. Introduce the Gated SAE, a modification to the standard SAE architecture that decouples detecting which features are present from estimating their magnitudes (Section 3.2);

2. Show that Gated SAEs Pareto improve the sparsity and reconstruction fidelity trade-off compared to baseline SAEs (Section 4.1);

3. Confirm that Gated SAEs overcome the shrinkage problem (Section 4.2), while outperforming other methods that also address this problem (Section 5.1);

4. Provide evidence from a small double-blind study that Gated SAE features are comparably interpretable to baseline SAE features (Section 4.3).

If these cosets are large enough, it is straightforward to finish breaking the cipher using frequency analysis, and there are examples that implement this technique. Park–Kim–Cho–Yum gave an improved version which is called the twist + algorithm. Millichap–Yau–Pate–Carns made further modifications to build the twist ++ algorithm. In this paper we give an accurate model for predicting the key length of a Vigenère cipher for a large range of key lengths and text lengths. Section 2 reviews a variety of well-established methods from the literature for predicting the key length of a Vigenère cipher and analyzes their strengths and weaknesses. title: Small-Space Algorithms for the Online Language Distance Problem for Palindromes and Squares

source.authors: Gabriel Bathie, Tomasz Kociumaka, Tatiana Starikovskaya

steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on small-space algorithms for the online language distance problem for palindromes and squares. It should introduce the language distance problem, define the online low-distance versions we study (Hamming and edit distance), state our streaming and read-only results, and end with a short related-work subsection.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. The language distance problem and prior work
2. Our setting: online, low-distance version for PAL and SQ
3. Formal problem definitions
4. Our results: streaming and read-only algorithms
5. Note on what is left out of this version
6. Related work (1.1): offline, online, streaming

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. The language distance problem and prior work
- one of the most fundamental problems in formal language theory
- task: minimal distance between a given string S and any string in a formal language L
- introduced early 1970s, Aho and Peterson
- studied extensively: regular languages (Hamming, edit distance); general context-free languages (mainly edit distance); Dyck language (well-nested parentheses sequences) in particular

2. Our setting
- complexity of the online + low-distance version
- given string T of length n; compute minimal distance from every prefix of T to L (distance and language fixed by the problem definition)
- low-distance regime: threshold k, distances larger than k need not be computed
- edit distance (min # character insertions, deletions, substitutions); Hamming distance (substitutions only) as preliminary step
- PAL = all palindromes (string equal to its reversed copy)
- SQ = all squares (concatenation of two copies of a string)
- similar yet very different: PAL not regular but context-free; SQ not even context-free

3. Definitions
- k - LHD - PAL (resp. k - LHD - SQ): input T of length n, positive integer k; output for each 1\leq i\leq n: \min\{k+1,hd_{i}\}, hd_{i} = min Hamming distance between the length-i prefix of T and a string in PAL (resp. SQ)
- k - LED - PAL (resp. k - LED - SQ): same, with edit distance ed_{i}

4. Results
- Amir and Porat: randomised streaming algorithm for k - LHD - PAL, \tilde{O}(k) space, \tilde{O}(k^{2}) time per input character
- we continue their line: streaming algorithms for all four problems, \poly(k,\log n) time per character, \poly(k,\log n) space
- streaming = extremely efficient (space counts everything, incl. info about the input), but randomised: may be wrong with probability inverse polynomial in n
- hence also read-only model: random access to input, not counted in space
- deterministic algorithms for all four, \poly(k,\log n) time per character and \poly(k,\log n) space; summary in Table 1
- side result: first \poly(k,\log n) space read-only algorithms for k -mismatch and k -edit occurrences of a pattern in a text

5. Omitted
- algorithms for k - LED - PAL and k - LED - SQ left out (lack of space), in the full version

6. Related work
- offline: all maximal substrings within Hamming distance k from PAL in O(nk) time (kangaroo jumps); edit distance O(nk^{2}), Porto and Barbosa; SQ: O(nk\log k+\mathrm{output}) Hamming, O(nk\log^{2}k+\mathrm{output}) edit
- online: k - LHD - PAL and k - LED - PAL generalize classical online palindrome recognition
- streaming: Berebrink et al., then Gawrychowski et al.: length of maximal substring of a stream in PAL; Merkurev and Shur: similar question for SQ

The language distance problem is a very fundamental problem in formal language theory. The task is to compute the minimal distance between a given string S and any string that belongs to a formal language L. It was introduced in the early 1970s by Aho and Peterson and has been studied a lot since then, for regular languages under Hamming and edit distances, for general context-free languages (mostly edit distance), and in particular for the Dyck language, which is the language of well-nested parentheses sequences.

In this work we study the complexity of the online and low-distance version of the problem. We are given a string T of length n and need to compute the minimal distance from every prefix of T to a formal language L (the problem definition says which distance and which language). We focus on the low-distance regime, so we assume there is a threshold parameter k and distances larger than k don't have to be computed. We consider the edit distance, which is the minimum number of character insertions, deletions and substitutions to transform one string into the other, and as a preliminary step the Hamming distance, which only allows substitutions. We look at two classical languages: the language PAL of all palindromes (a palindrome is a string that is equal to its reversed copy) and the language SQ of all squares (a square is two copies of a string concatenated). These languages are very similar but also very different in nature: PAL is context-free but not regular, and SQ is not even context-free. Formally the problems are as follows:

k - LHD - PAL (resp. k - LHD - SQ) Input: A string T of length n and a positive integer k. Output: For each 1\leq i\leq n, report \min\{k+1,hd_{i}\}, where hd_{i} is the minimum Hamming distance between the prefix of T of length i and a string in PAL (resp. in SQ).

k - LED - PAL (resp. k - LED - SQ) Input: A string T of length n and a positive integer k. Output: For each 1\leq i\leq n, report \min\{k+1,ed_{i}\}, where ed_{i} is the minimum edit distance between the prefix of T of length i and a string in PAL (resp. in SQ).

[Results]
- Amir and Porat: randomised streaming algorithm for k - LHD - PAL in \tilde{O}(k) space, \tilde{O}(k^{2}) time per input character
- we continue: streaming algorithms for all four problems, \poly(k,\log n) time per character and \poly(k,\log n) space
- streaming is extremely efficient (space includes info about the input) but randomised, may be wrong w.p. inverse polynomial in n
- so also read-only model (random access to input, not counted in space): deterministic algorithms for all four, \poly(k,\log n) time per character and space; Table 1
- side result: first \poly(k,\log n) space read-only algorithms for k -mismatch and k -edit occurrences of a pattern in a text

[Omitted] LED algorithms (k - LED - PAL, k - LED - SQ) not in this version for lack of space, see full version

## 1.1 Related work.
- Offline: Hamming distance k from PAL, all maximal substrings in O(nk), kangaroo jumps; edit distance O(nk^{2}) by Porto and Barbosa; SQ: O(nk\log k+\mathrm{output}) Hamming, O(nk\log^{2}k+\mathrm{output}) edit
- Online: generalization of classical online palindrome recognition
- Streaming: Berebrink et al., then Gawrychowski et al. (maximal substring of a stream in PAL); Merkurev and Shur (SQ)

We show streaming algorithms for all four problems, and they use \poly(k,\log n) time per character and \poly(k,\log n) space. Because of this we also study the problems in the read-only model. In this model random access to the input is allowed and it is not counted in the space usage. Because of the lack of space, the descriptions of the algorithms for the Language edit distance problems (k - LED - PAL and k - LED - SQ) are not in this version of the paper. They can be found in the full version.

## 1.1 Related work.

Offline model. In the classical offline model, finding all maximal substrings that are within Hamming distance k from PAL can be done in O(nk) time, which is a simple application of the kangaroo jumps technique. Streaming algorithms for PAL and SQ. Berebrink et al. and after them Gawrychowski et al. studied how to compute the length of a maximal substring of a stream that belongs to PAL. Merkurev and Shur looked at a similar question for the SQ language.

steps.name: final
steps.text:
The language distance problem is one of the most fundamental problems in formal language theory. In this problem, the task is to compute the minimal distance between a given string S and any string belonging to a formal language L. Introduced in the early 1970s by Aho and Peterson [1], the language distance problem has been studied extensively for regular languages under Hamming and edit distances [2], for general context-free languages, mainly focusing on the edit distance [3,1,4,5,6,7,8,9,10,11], and the Dyck language (the language of well-nested parentheses sequences) in particular [3,12,4,5,13,14,15,16,17,18,9,10].

In this work, we study the complexity of the online and low-distance version of the language distance problem, where we are given a string T of length n, and the task is to compute the minimal distance from every prefix of T to a formal language L (the distance and the language are specified in the problem definition). We focus on the low-distance regime, i.e., we assume to be given a threshold parameter k such that distances larger than k do not need to be computed. We consider the edit distance (defined as the minimum number of character insertions, deletions, and substitutions needed to transform one string into the other) and, as a preliminary step, the Hamming distance (allowing for substitutions only). We study the problem for two classical languages: the language PAL of all palindromes, where a palindrome is a string that is equal to its reversed copy, and the language SQ of all squares, where a square is the concatenation of two copies of a string. These two languages are very similar yet very different in nature: PAL is not regular but is context-free, whereas SQ is not even context-free. Formally, the problems we consider are defined as follows:

k - LHD - PAL (resp. k - LHD - SQ) Input: A string T of length n and a positive integer k. Output: For each 1\leq i\leq n, report \min\{k+1,hd_{i}\}, where hd_{i} is the minimum Hamming distance between T[1.\,.i] and a string in PAL (resp. in SQ).

k - LED - PAL (resp. k - LED - SQ) Input: A string T of length n and a positive integer k. Output: For each 1\leq i\leq n, report \min\{k+1,ed_{i}\}, where ed_{i} is the minimum edit distance between T[1.\,.i] and a string in PAL (resp. in SQ).

Amir and Porat [19] showed that there is a randomised streaming algorithm that solves the k - LHD - PAL problem in \tilde{O}(k) space and \tilde{O}(k^{2}) time per input character. We continue their line of research and show streaming algorithms for all four problems that use \poly(k,\log n) time per character and \poly(k,\log n) space. While streaming algorithms are extremely efficient (in particular, the space complexities above account for all the space used by the algorithms, including the space needed to store information about the input), it is important to note that they are randomised in nature, which means that they may produce incorrect results with a certain probability (inverse polynomial in the input size n). Motivated by this, we also study the problems in the read-only model, where random access to the input is allowed (and not accounted for in the space usage). In this model, we show deterministic algorithms for the four problems that use \poly(k,\log n) time per character and \poly(k,\log n) space; see Table 1 for a summary. As a side result of independent interest, we develop the first \poly(k,\log n) space read-only algorithms for computing k -mismatch and k -edit occurrences of a pattern in a text.

Due to the lack of space, descriptions of the algorithms for the Language edit distance problems (k - LED - PAL and k - LED - SQ) are omitted from this version of the paper, but can be found in the full one.

## 1.1 Related work.

Offline model. In the classical offline model, the problem of finding all maximal substrings that are within Hamming distance k from PAL can be solved in O(nk) time as a simple application of the kangaroo jumps technique [20]. For the edit distance, Porto and Barbosa [21] showed an O(nk^{2}) solution. For the SQ language, the best known solutions take O(nk\log k+\mathrm{output}) time for the Hamming distance [22] and O(nk\log^{2}k+\mathrm{output}) for the edit distance [23,24,25].

Online model. The problems k - LHD - PAL and k - LED - PAL can be viewed as a generalization of the classical online palindrome recognition problem (see [26] and references therein).

Streaming algorithms for PAL and SQ. Berebrink et al. [27] followed by Gawrychowski et al. [28] studied the question of computing the length of a maximal substring of a stream that belongs to PAL. Merkurev and Shur [29] considered a similar question for the SQ language.

title: Shining Light into the Tunnel: Understanding and Classifying Network Traffic of Residential Proxies

source.authors: Ronghong Huang, Dongfang Zhao, Xianghang Mi, Xiaofeng Wang

steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our security paper on residential proxies (RESIPs), about understanding and classifying the network traffic they relay. Cover what RESIPs are and what earlier work found, what we did and the challenges we solved, our key findings, and end with a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Background: what RESIPs are; prior work on their scale and recruitment
2. Prior work on RESIP abuse and on detecting RESIP traffic, and its gaps
3. What this paper contributes: dataset, ML classifiers, traffic analysis
4. Methodology and challenges: collecting traffic via bandwidth sharing, analyzer, classifiers
5. Key findings: sensitive websites, email spam, early-time detection
6. Contributions list

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Background
- RESIPs = web proxies located in residential or cellular networks
- vs traditional web proxies (VPNs, open web proxies): much larger scale, wider distribution (previous studies)
- recruitment by RESIP services studied -> controversial / malicious channels: PUPs installed on Windows devices; mobile proxy apps with ambiguous user consent prompts

2. Prior work on abuse and detection
- Mi et al.: traffic logs of PUPs confirmed as RESIPs -> malicious traffic of multiple categories (advertisement frauds, blackhat SEO)
- gap: unclear if PUP logs are only RESIP traffic; PUPs may have other malicious functions
- RESIP traffic relayed by mobile proxy apps captured and analyzed -> suspicious traffic, similar categories
- gap: scale of captured traffic not specified, traffic not released
- detection: some studies target relayed flows; others tunnel connections between RESIP node and RESIP gateway server (tunnel flows)
- gap: none evaluated on wild RESIP traffic

3. This paper
- largest-ever dataset: over 3TB RESIP traffic, over 116 million flows, destinations of 188K IP addresses and 116K FQDNs
- ML for relayed + tunnel flows: relayed classifier recall 88.80%, precision 96.20%; tunnel classifier recall 91.39%, precision 95.71%
- in-depth analysis of relayed flows -> novel findings on abuse

4. Methodology / challenges
- challenge 1: collect RESIP traffic at scale; RESIP services keep RESIPs as black boxes
- some RESIP providers also run bandwidth sharing (BS) as a service: PacketStream, IPRoyal, Honeygain
- BS: monetize idle bandwidth of a BS node (e.g., laptop); operator paid in proportion to bandwidth contributed
- preliminary experiments: BS bandwidth exclusively relays RESIP traffic -> BS nodes = RESIP nodes
- deploy BS nodes at scale; also: triggering effective BS (RESIP) traffic, scalable deployment + collection -> general RESIP traffic collector
- RESIP traffic analyzer: efficient processing, locate inherent security risks
- robust features + multiple ML classifiers: early-time detection of relayed and tunnel flows, high precision

5. Key findings
- first time: RESIPs used extensively to masquerade attackers as local residents on sensitive websites (government, military, other public sector)
- 73 security-sensitive websites: industrial control systems, airport control systems, watering control systems, remote desktops inside government agencies, military websites
- 31% governments, 18% military agencies, 21% other public sector (hospitals, education agencies, railway management companies, research agencies)
- strong correlation: country of our RESIP nodes vs country hosting the websites
- first time: large volume of email spamming + suspicious email retrieving relayed
- 465K sender addresses, 2.29 million recipient addresses, 549K unique spam messages
- evasion: text paraphrasing, complicated combinations of character encodings, email encodings, homoglyphs
- transformer-based classifiers: no manual feature engineering, first 5 packets only; relayed: recall 93.04%, precision 92.87%
- feature-based models: better explainability, decent performance; first 4 upstream packets, tunnel: recall 91.94%, precision 94.87%
- first work applying ML to RESIP traffic detection

6. Contributions
- methodology to collect RESIP traffic at large scale and analyze it for security risks
- largest-ever dataset of wild RESIP traffic, available upon request (foster research, avoid security/privacy risks)
- analyzer -> multiple novel and concerning findings on malicious usage
- first demonstration that ML for RESIP traffic detection is feasible

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Residential proxies (RESIPs) are web proxies located in residential or cellular networks. Previous studies showed that compared to traditional web proxies, like VPNs and open web proxies, RESIPs have a much larger scale and a wider distribution. Because of this large scale, previous studies looked at how RESIP services recruit RESIPs, and found multiple recruitment channels that are controversial or even malicious, for example installing potentially unwanted programs (PUPs) on Windows devices and distributing mobile proxy apps with ambiguous user consent prompts.

Research has also tried to understand the usage (abuse) of RESIPs. Mi et al. used traffic logs of PUPs that were confirmed to serve as RESIPs and found malicious RESIP traffic of multiple categories, such as advertisement frauds and blackhat search engine optimization (SEO). But it is not clear if the PUP traffic logs are only RESIP traffic, since the PUPs can have other malicious functions at the same time that may contribute to the malicious logs. RESIP traffic relayed by mobile proxy apps was also captured and analyzed, and suspicious traffic of similar categories was observed, but the authors did not say how much RESIP traffic they captured and they did not release it to the public. Since RESIPs are abused in many malicious activities, there have also been efforts to detect RESIP traffic. Some studies looked at traffic flows relayed by RESIPs (relayed flows) and others at the tunnel connections between a RESIP node and a RESIP gateway server (tunnel flows). But none of these methods was evaluated on wild RESIP traffic.

This paper goes further than these studies and contributes in several aspects. First, we collected the largest-ever dataset of RESIP traffic, over 3TB, with over 116 million traffic flows going to traffic destinations of 188K IP addresses and 116K fully qualified domain names. This dataset of wild RESIP traffic also lets us explore whether machine learning can be applied to detect both relayed flows and tunnel flows. We built multiple machine learning classifiers which got very good performance: the relayed flow classifier has a recall of 88.80% and a precision of 96.20%, and the tunnel flow classifier has 91.39% recall and 95.71% precision. We also did an in-depth analysis of the flows relayed by RESIPs, which gave multiple novel findings about how RESIPs are abused in malicious activities.

[Methodology / challenges]
- collecting RESIP traffic at scale is hard, RESIP services keep RESIPs as black boxes
- some RESIP providers also operate bandwidth sharing (BS) as a service; representative BS providers: PacketStream, IPRoyal, Honeygain
- BS = monetize idle bandwidth on a BS node (e.g., a laptop device); operator paid proportional to bandwidth contributed
- preliminary experiments: bandwidth of BS nodes exclusively relays RESIP traffic, i.e. BS nodes are RESIP nodes
- so we deploy BS nodes at scale; other challenges: triggering effective BS (RESIP) traffic, deploying nodes and collecting traffic in a scalable way -> general RESIP traffic collector
- RESIP traffic analyzer: process traffic efficiently, locate the inherent security risks
- robust features + multiple ML classifiers for early-time detection of relayed and tunnel flows with high precision

[Key findings]
- first time: RESIPs used extensively to masquerade attackers as local residents visiting sensitive websites of government agencies, military agencies, other public sector organizations
- suspicious flows to 73 security-sensitive websites (industrial control systems, airport control systems, watering control systems, remote desktops inside government agencies, military websites); 31% government, 18% military, 21% other public sector (hospitals, education agencies, railway management companies, research agencies)
- strong correlation between country of our RESIP nodes and country where the websites are hosted
- first time: large volume of email spamming and suspicious email retrieving relayed; 465K sender addresses, 2.29 million recipients, 549K unique spam messages; evasion: text paraphrasing, complicated combinations of character encodings, email encodings, homoglyphs
- transformer-based classifiers: no manual feature engineering, only first 5 packets; relayed: recall 93.04%, precision 92.87%
- feature-based models: better explainability, decent performance; first 4 upstream packets, tunnel: recall 91.94%, precision 94.87%
- first work applying ML to RESIP traffic detection

[Contributions]
- novel methodology to collect RESIP traffic at large scale and analyze it for security risks
- largest-ever dataset of wild RESIP traffic, available upon request
- analyzer: multiple novel, concerning findings on malicious usage of RESIPs
- first to show ML is feasible for detecting RESIP traffic

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Residential proxies (RESIPs) are web proxies that are located in residential networks or in cellular networks. Previous studies have shown that RESIPs, compared to traditional web proxies like VPNs and open web proxies, tend to have a much larger scale and also a wider distribution. Because the scale is so large, previous studies have looked into how RESIP services recruit RESIPs, and this led to discovering multiple recruitment channels that are controversial or even malicious, for example installing potentially unwanted programs (PUPs) on Windows devices, distributing mobile proxy apps that have ambiguous user consent prompts, etc.

There has also been research to understand the usage (abuse) of RESIPs. Mi, et al. used traffic logs of PUPs that were confirmed to serve as RESIPs and discovered malicious RESIP traffic of multiple categories, like advertisement frauds and blackhat search engine optimization (SEO). But it is not clear if the PUP traffic logs are only RESIP traffic, because these PUPs can have other malicious functionalities at the same time, and these could also contribute to the malicious traffic logs. Also, RESIP traffic relayed by mobile proxy apps had been captured and analyzed, and suspicious traffic of similar categories was observed in it. However the authors did not specify the scale of the RESIP traffic they captured, and they did not release the RESIP traffic to the public. Since RESIPs are abused in various malicious activities, there have been further efforts to detect RESIP traffic. Some studies targeted traffic flows that are relayed by RESIPs, which are called relayed flows, and others focused on the tunnel connections between a RESIP node and a RESIP gateway server, which are called tunnel flows. However none of these methodologies was evaluated on wild RESIP traffic.

This paper goes further than these previous studies and it makes contributions in several aspects. First, we collected the largest-ever dataset of RESIP traffic, which is over 3TB, and it has over 116 million traffic flows going to traffic destinations of 188K IP addresses and 116K fully qualified domain names. Also, this dataset of wild RESIP traffic gives us the opportunity to see if it is feasible to apply machine learning to detecting both relayed flows and tunnel flows. We built multiple machine learning classifiers and they got very good performance. Our relayed flow classifier got a recall of 88.80% and a precision of 96.20%, and our tunnel flow classifier got 91.39% recall and 95.71% precision. We also did an in-depth analysis of the traffic flows relayed by RESIPs, and the analysis gave multiple novel findings about how RESIPs are abused in malicious activities.

To do this study we had to design and implement a set of novel methodologies. The first challenge we had was how to collect RESIP traffic at scale, especially since RESIP services are known to keep their RESIPs as black boxes. We observe that some RESIP providers are also operating bandwidth sharing (BS) as a service at the same time. The representative BS providers we studied include PacketStream, IPRoyal, and Honeygain. A BS service is offered to monetize the idle bandwidth on a BS node (e.g., a laptop device), and the node operator gets paid in proportion to how much bandwidth the node contributed. We ran BS nodes in preliminary experiments and analyzed the traffic that came out, and we confirmed that the bandwidth provided by BS nodes is used only to relay RESIP traffic. So BS nodes are used exclusively as RESIP nodes. Therefore we collected RESIP traffic by deploying BS nodes at scale. While doing this we also had to address other challenges, like how to trigger effective BS (RESIP) traffic and how to deploy BS nodes and collect the traffic in a scalable way, and together these lead to a general RESIP traffic collector. Then we built a RESIP traffic analyzer that processes RESIP traffic efficiently and locates the inherent security risks effectively. Our in-depth analysis of RESIP traffic found a set of novel and concerning security findings, which we highlight below. Since the security risks of RESIP traffic are concerning, we also designed a set of robust features and built multiple machine learning classifiers, which enable early-time detection of both relayed flows and tunnel flows with high precision.

Below we summarize the key findings and contributions of this study.

First, we observe for the first time that RESIPs have been used extensively to masquerade attackers as local residents when they visit sensitive websites that are operated by government agencies, military agencies, and organizations in other public sectors. In total we observed suspicious traffic flows to 73 different security-sensitive websites. These websites belong to diverse categories, for example industrial control systems, airport control systems, watering control systems, remote desktops inside government agencies, and various military websites. Of these websites, 31% are operated by governments, 18% are for military agencies, and another 21% are for other organizations in the public sector, e.g., hospitals, education agencies, railway management companies, and research agencies. We also observe a strong correlation between the country of our RESIP nodes and the country where these sensitive websites are hosted.

Also for the first time, we confirm that RESIPs have been used to relay a large volume of email spamming activities and also suspicious email retrieving activities. The email spamming activities involve 465K sender email addresses, 2.29 million recipient email addresses, and 549K unique spam messages. We also observe that email spammers use various evasion techniques, e.g., text paraphrasing, complicated combinations of character encodings, email encodings, homoglyphs, etc.

Next, we built a set of machine learning classifiers to enable early-time detection of RESIP traffic, and they show good performance. Our transformer-based classifiers remove the burden of manual feature engineering, and they also get high detection performance while only taking in the first 5 packets of each traffic flow. [citation needed] used traffic logs of PUPs that were confirmed to serve as RESIPs and discovered malicious RESIP traffic of multiple categories, like advertisement frauds and blackhat search engine optimization (SEO). Some studies [citation needed] targeted traffic flows that are relayed by RESIPs, which are called relayed flows, and others [citation needed] focused on the tunnel connections between a RESIP node and a RESIP gateway server, which are called tunnel flows. However none of these methodologies was evaluated on wild RESIP traffic.

This paper goes further than these previous studies and it makes contributions in several aspects. First, we collected the largest-ever dataset of RESIP traffic, which is over 3TB, and it has over 116 million traffic flows going to traffic destinations of 188K IP addresses and 116K fully qualified domain names. For example, when only the first 4 upstream packets are considered, our feature-based model for tunnel flow classification can get a recall of 91.94% and a precision of 94.87%. For example, propagate-values is a tactic in Z3 that propagates equalities, and sat and smt are tactics that wrap the main SAT and SMT solver in Z3. A strategy combines tactics to build a decision procedure, for example the strategy (if is-pb (then propagate-values sat) smt). What this strategy does is, given an input instance, it applies propagate-values and then sat if the instance is a pseudo-boolean problem (which is checked with is-pb), and otherwise it applies smt.

The default strategies of solvers are usually optimized for well-established benchmarks, for example the ones in the SMT-LIB library. But the scope of SMT applications is growing fast, and users often run into classes of instances that are specialized, evolving, and unprecedented. For these, the default strategies or the existing customized strategies might not work as well. So there is a need for new customized strategies that are designed specifically to handle the unique challenges of the users' specific problems efficiently. Usually this strategy customization has been done by human experts, who do a lot of experiments and benchmark analysis. But even for experts putting in lots of effort this is still hard, because tactics interact in intricate ways and the search space of possible strategies is very large.

There have been some early attempts to synthesize SMT strategies automatically. StratEVO uses evolutionary algorithms to search for an optimal strategy, and FastSMT uses imitation learning and decision tree learning to synthesize a tailored strategy. These methods are promising for automating strategy customization, but they have problems such as not being robust, limited interpretability, and long training times.

To deal with these problems, we introduce a new SMT strategy synthesis method that uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). MCTS is a heuristic search algorithm that is widely used in computer board game players as a lookahead planning algorithm. It became even more prominent after it was successfully integrated into the deep reinforcement learning systems AlphaGo and AlphaZero, which were groundbreaking, and where MCTS was used as a policy improvement operator. Recently MCTS has also been very successful as a standalone algorithm for solving complex symbolic or combinatorial search problems, for example in Khalil et al. and Sun et al.. Its main strengths are that it balances exploration and exploitation effectively and that it adapts to the nuances of different search problems, which makes it a great method for these kinds of hard tasks. Our work is the first one to apply MCTS to the SMT strategy synthesis problem.

## 1.1 The Strategy Synthesis Problem

The SMT strategy synthesis problem is to automatically find an optimal strategy that gives the best performance on a given benchmark set P. Performance is usually measured with metrics like the number of instances in P that are solved within a given wallclock timeout t. P is supposed to be a representative subset of a larger benchmark set Q that the user is interested in, and the expectation is that a strategy that does well on P will also generalize well to Q. Note that because the strategy search space is infinite and strategies are evaluated empirically, it is not practical to find a rigorously optimal solution. So our goal is to find a near-optimal solution in a reasonable search time, based on empirical measurements. In this research we focus on strategy synthesis for Z3, which is widely regarded as one of the most prevalent SMT solvers that are used today.

## 1.2 Our Contributions

1. Z3alpha, an MCTS-based strategy synthesizing solver: We present a new framework based on MCTS, which we call Z3alpha, for the SMT strategy synthesis problem. It automatically constructs solver strategies that are tailored to a given class of problem instances. As far as we know, Z3alpha is the first MCTS-based method for the SMT strategy synthesis problem.

2. Layered and staged MCTS: Strategy synthesis has some unique challenges that conventional MCTS alone cannot solve, so we develop two new heuristics on top of the MCTS framework, layered search and staged search. Layered search narrows the search space by treating some auxiliary tasks as independent search problems. Staged search splits the whole search problem into sequential sub-problems, so that results from the early stages can be used to speed up the search in the later stages. The two techniques work together to make the search for the optimal strategy more efficient and effective, which is important since evaluating strategies takes a lot of time.

3. Extensive experimental evaluation: We implemented Z3alpha on top of the leading SMT solver Z3. We did comprehensive experiments to evaluate its performance, comparing Z3alpha to the state-of-the-art (SOTA) synthesis tool FastSMT, and also to Z3's own handcrafted default strategy and to the CVC5 solver. The experiments covered instances from six different SMT logics (QF_{BV, LIA, LRA, NIA, NRA, S}), with a wide range of problem sizes and solver runtimes. In all of the experiments Z3alpha showed superior and robust performance. This shows the benefits of automatic strategy customization and promotes broader adoption of user-controllable strategies in the SMT community.

Because the strategy search space is infinite and strategies are evaluated empirically, finding a rigorously optimal solution is impractical. Our objective is therefore to discover a near-optimal solution within a reasonable search time, based on empirical measurements. This work focuses on strategy synthesis for Z3, which is widely regarded as one of the most prevalent SMT solvers in use today.

## 1.2 Our Contributions

1. Z3alpha: An MCTS-based Strategy Synthesizing Solver: We present a novel MCTS-based framework, called Z3alpha, for the SMT strategy synthesis problem, which automatically constructs tailored solver strategies for a given class of problem instances. To the best of our knowledge, Z3alpha is the first MCTS-based method for the SMT strategy synthesis problem.

2. Layered and Staged MCTS: To address challenges of strategy synthesis that conventional MCTS alone cannot solve, we develop two new heuristics on top of the MCTS framework: layered search and staged search. Layered search narrows the search space by treating certain auxiliary tasks as independent search problems. Staged search, on the other hand, divides the whole search problem into sequential sub-problems, so that results from early stages can speed up the search in later stages. Together, the two techniques improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the search for the optimal strategy, which is essential given how time-consuming strategy evaluations are.

3. Extensive Experimental Evaluation: We implemented Z3alpha on top of the leading SMT solver Z3 and conducted comprehensive experiments comparing it with the state-of-the-art (SOTA) synthesis tool FastSMT, as well as with Z3's own handcrafted default strategy and the CVC5 solver. The experiments covered instances from six different SMT logics (namely, QF_{BV, LIA, LRA, NIA, NRA, S}), representing a wide range of problem sizes and solver runtimes. Across all experiments, Z3alpha consistently showed superior and robust performance. These results highlight the benefits of automatic strategy customization and should promote broader adoption of user-controllable strategies in the SMT community.

steps.text:
Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solvers [1] are key tools in diverse fields such as software engineering [2], verification [3], security [4], and artificial intelligence [5]. It has long been observed that no single solver or algorithm excels across all instances of a given SMT logic or of a problem class. As a result, modern SMT solvers, such as Z3 [6], offer user-controllable strategies [7], enabling users to customize a decision procedure for their class of instances. A strategy can be thought of as an algorithmic recipe for selecting, sequencing, and parameterizing tactics. Each tactic is a well-defined algorithmic proof rule or symbolic reasoning step, provided by the solver. For example, propagate-values is a Z3 tactic that propagates equalities, while sat and smt are the tactic wrappers of the main SAT and SMT solver in Z3. A strategy builds a decision procedure by combining tactics, as shown in an exemplar strategy (if is-pb (then propagate-values sat) smt). This strategy specifies a solving algorithm that, given an input instance, applies propagate-values followed by sat if the instance is a pseudo-boolean problem (as checked using is-pb), or applies smt otherwise.

Default solver strategies are typically optimized for well-established benchmarks, such as those in the SMT-LIB library [8]. However, as the scope of SMT applications continues to grow rapidly, users frequently encounter specialized, evolving, and unprecedented classes of instances. In these scenarios, the default or the existing customized strategies might not be as effective. Consequently, there arises a need for novel customized strategies, specifically designed to efficiently address the unique challenges posed by users’ specific problems. Traditionally, this task of strategy customization has been undertaken by human experts through extensive experimentation and benchmark analysis. However, even with their expertise and efforts, the task remains challenging due to the intricate interactions among tactics and the vast search space for potential strategies.

Early attempts have been made to synthesize SMT strategies automatically. For instance, StratEVO [9] searches for an optimal strategy using evolutionary algorithms, while FastSMT [10] synthesizes a tailored strategy using imitation learning and decision tree learning techniques. While these methods show promise in automating strategy customization, they suffer from issues such as a lack of robustness, limited interpretability, and extensive training times.

To address these issues, we introduce a novel SMT strategy synthesis method that employs Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). MCTS is a heuristic search algorithm, widely applied in computer board game players as a lookahead planning algorithm [11]. Its prominence further escalated following its successful integration into the groundbreaking deep reinforcement learning systems AlphaGo [12] and AlphaZero [13], where MCTS was employed as a policy improvement operator. Recently, MCTS has shown remarkable success as a standalone algorithm in solving complex symbolic or combinatorial search problems, as evidenced in Khalil et al. [14] and Sun et al. [15]. Its key strengths, including its ability to effectively balance exploration and exploitation and its adaptiveness to the nuances of varied search problems, make it an excellent method for such challenging tasks. Our work is the first to apply MCTS to the SMT strategy synthesis problem.

## 1.1 The Strategy Synthesis Problem

The SMT strategy synthesis problem is defined as automatically identifying an optimal strategy that yields the best performance for a given benchmark set P. This performance is typically measured in terms of metrics such as the number of P -instances successfully solved within a specified wallclock timeout t. P is intended to be a representative subset of the broader benchmark set Q, which is of interest to the user, with the expectation that a strategy performing well on P generalizes effectively to Q. It is important to note that due to the infinite nature of the strategy search space and the empirical approach to strategy evaluation, finding a rigorously optimal solution is impractical. Consequently, our objective is to discover a near-optimal solution within a reasonable search time, based on empirical measurements. This research focuses on strategy synthesis for Z3, a solver that is widely regarded as one of the most prevalent SMT solvers in use today.

## 1.2 Our Contributions

- 1. Z3alpha: An MCTS-based Strategy Synthesizing Solver: We present a novel MCTS-based framework, dubbed Z3alpha, for the SMT strategy synthesis problem, which automatically constructs tailored solver strategies for a given class of problem instances. To the best of our knowledge, Z3alpha is the first MCTS-based method developed for the SMT strategy synthesis problem.

- 2. Layered and Staged MCTS: To address the unique challenges inherent to strategy synthesis, that cannot be solved by the conventional MCTS alone, we develop two innovative heuristics, namely, layered search and staged search on top of the MCTS framework. The layered search method effectively narrows the search space by treating certain auxiliary tasks as independent search problems. On the other hand, the staged search technique segments the entire search problem into sequential sub-problems, enabling the use of results from early stages to expedite the search in later stages. Together, these two techniques work symbiotically to enhance the search efficiency and effectiveness in finding the optimal strategy, an essential improvement given the time-consuming nature of strategy evaluations.

- 3. Extensive Experimental Evaluation: We implemented our proposed method, dubbed Z3alpha, on top of the leading SMT solver Z3. To assess its performance, we conducted comprehensive experiments, comparing Z3alpha with the state-of-the-art (SOTA) synthesis tool FastSMT, as well as Z3 ’s own handcrafted default strategy and the CVC5 solver. These experiments spanned a broad spectrum, including instances from six different SMT logics (namely, QF_{BV, LIA, LRA, NIA, NRA, S}), representing a wide range of problem sizes and solver runtimes. Across all experiments, Z3alpha consistently demonstrated superior and robust performance. This impressive performance strongly highlights the benefits of automatic strategy customization, promoting broader adoption of user-controllable strategies within the SMT community.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
## Historical background: computational machinery
- Robin Gandy (1919–1995): student of Alan Turing (1912–1954), lifelong friend
- Gandy traces "calculating machine" back to Charles Babbage (circa 1834); proposes "Babbage's Thesis"
  - [quote: Babbage's Thesis, italics in Babbage as cited by Gandy]
- Gandy's analysis of the analytical engine: five operations (cf. p. 52–53)
  - arithmetic +, −, × ("proper" subtraction: x − y = 0 if y ≥ x)
  - any sequence of operations is an operation
  - iteration (repeat operation P n times)
  - conditional iteration (repeat P n times, conditional on "success" of test T)
  - conditional transfer (conditional "goto")
- Gandy: functions calculable by (1), (2), (4) = exactly the Turing computable ones
- other "universal calculating machines": Percy Ludgate (1909), Leonardo Torres Quevedo (1914), Maurice d'Ocagne (1922), Louis Couffignal (1933), Vannevar Bush (1936), Howard Aiken (1937)
  - [quote: Gandy — emphasis on fixed arithmetic sequences; conditional iteration/transfer not recognized]

## The Entscheidungsproblem (the "decision problem"): Hilbert's tenth question of 1900
- David Hilbert's problems, 1900; an aspect of #10 floating about for almost 30 years before framed precisely
  - [quote: Hilbert's original No. 10 + the Entscheidungsproblem; translation in Dershowitz and Gurevich, 2008]
- 1922: H. Behmann on the "most general form" of the Entscheidungsproblem
  - [quotes via Gandy: definite prescription, finite steps; equivalent to deciding which propositions are true; would give a procedure for solving many/all problems]
- 1928 international congress of mathematicians: Hilbert's questions made precise — complete? consistent? decidable?
  - first two answered 1930 by Kurt Gödel, at the same meeting as Hilbert's retirement speech (chagrin)
  - third (Entscheidungsproblem) waits until mid-1930s
- needs precise definition of "definite general applicable prescription" (Church: "effective calculability"); none in 1928
- next 6–7 years:
  - Emil Post: worker moving room to room, writing/erasing marks per list of instructions
  - Church + students Stephen Kleene, J. B. Rosser: lambda-calculus, Gödel's recursion theory (1934)
- Church's paper (15 April 1936): Entscheidungsproblem "undecidable"; beat Turing by almost a year (Turing submitted 28 May 1936, published January 1937)
- Post: brief paper, fall 1936 -> Turing has priority over Post
- Church referees Turing's paper; Turing studies Church's, adds Appendix sketching proof that lambda-calculus and his machines compute same functions
  - [quote: Hodges — Church's result weaker; Turing's more direct, from first principles]
- Post only proposed a definition, criticised Church's, proved nothing

## Alan Turing's a-machine
- spring 1935: Turing, young Master's student, King's College, Cambridge, takes on the challenge
- stimulated by lectures of logician M. H. A. Newman (Gödel's work, Entscheidungsproblem, "mechanical")
  - [quote: Newman's 1955 obituary of Turing, via Gandy — "Something that can be done by a machine"]
  - [quote: Gandy — undecidability as goal from the start? 'main idea' in Grantchester meadows, summer 1935]
- Gandy: Newman's statement "misleading"; not shared by all
- lifelong interest in machines: typewriters as a boy, Mrs. Turing's typewriter, "mechanical" (Hodges p. 96)
- at Princeton (PhD): Boolean-logic multiplier (see below)
- PhD thesis "Systems of Logic Based on Ordinals": definition of "a computable function"
  - [quote: Turing (1939, p. 166) — purely mechanical process; three definitions equivalent]
- 1936: invents "a-machine" (automatic machine)
- paper submitted 31 May 1936 to London Mathematical Society (Proceedings); published early 1937; offprints February 1937
- term "Turing machine" coined later by Church (doctoral advisor) in a review
- two questions answered in the negative:
  - machine deciding whether any arbitrary machine on its tape is "circular" (freezes / fails to continue)?
  - machine deciding whether any arbitrary machine on its tape ever prints a given symbol?
- simple device, arbitrary computations -> properties of computation in general; uncomputability of Entscheidungsproblem
- back in UK: jointly responsible for breaking German "Enigma" codes; ACE (Automatic Computing Engine)
  - Hodges p. 318: ACE roots in his own universal machine, not EDVAC
- Kleene (1952) names "Turing's Thesis"; arguments continue on origin and nature
- what Turing did prove: "On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem" (1937)
  - [quote: Turing — no general process for whether formula U of functional calculus K is provable; The Undecidable, p. 145]
- second proof: "Does this machine ever print 0" is "undecidable"

## 1937–1970: The "digital computer", the birth of "computer science"
- 1937, Princeton: digital (Boolean-logic) multiplier from scratch, own electromechanical relays (Hodges p. 138)
  - Hodges p. 138: logical design of a Turing machine in relay-operated switches
- earnest work elsewhere: Konrad Zuse (1938), Germany; Howard Aiken, George Stibitz (1937), US; used by Axis and Allied militaries in WWII (Hodges p. 298–299)
- early–mid 1950s: Hao Wang, Marvin Minsky reduce TM to simpler form (precursor of Martin Davis's Post–Turing machine); Europeans reduce electronic computer to theoretical object equivalent to TM
- late 1950s/early 1960s: Melzak and Lambek (1961), Minsky (1961), Shepherdson and Sturgis (1961) -> counter machine
- Elgot and Robinson (1964), Hartmanis (1971), Cook and Reckhow (1973) -> register machine, random-access machine
- all basically multi-tape TMs with arithmetic-like instruction set

- counter, register, random-access machines + their sire the TM: models of choice in theory of computation

  - [quote: Van Emde Boas (1990) — off-line multitape TM and RAM (Cook and Reckhow) dominant in machine-based complexity theory]
  - [quote: Van Emde Boas (1990) — RAM takes the role in analysis of algorithms]

## Historical background: computational machinery

Robin Gandy (1919–1995) was a student of Alan Turing (1912–1954), and also his lifelong friend. Gandy traces the idea of a "calculating machine" back to Charles Babbage (circa 1834), and he actually proposes something he calls "Babbage's Thesis":

> That the whole of development and operations of analysis are now capable of being executed by machinery.

— (italics in Babbage as cited by Gandy)

Gandy analyses Babbage's analytical engine and describes the following five operations that it has (cf. p. 52–53):

- The arithmetic functions +, −, ×, where − is "proper" subtraction: x − y = 0 if y ≥ x.
- Any sequence of operations is an operation.
- Iteration of an operation (repeating an operation P n times).
- Conditional iteration (repeating an operation P n times, conditional on the "success" of test T).
- Conditional transfer (i.e., a conditional "goto").

According to Gandy, "the functions which can be calculated by (1), (2), and (4) are precisely those which are Turing computable." He also cites other proposals for "universal calculating machines", which include the ones by Percy Ludgate (1909), Leonardo Torres Quevedo (1914), Maurice d'Ocagne (1922), Louis Couffignal (1933), Vannevar Bush (1936) and Howard Aiken (1937). But about these he says:

> … the emphasis is on programming a fixed iterable sequence of arithmetical operations. The fundamental importance of conditional iteration and conditional transfer for a general theory of calculating machines is not recognized…

— Gandy

## The Entscheidungsproblem (the "decision problem"): Hilbert's tenth question of 1900

The famous mathematician David Hilbert posed his problems in 1900, and one aspect of problem #10 had been floating around for almost 30 years before it got framed precisely. This is Hilbert's original expression for No. 10:

> 10. Determination of the solvability of a Diophantine equation. Given a Diophantine equation with any number of unknown quantities and with rational integral coefficients: To devise a process according to which it can be determined in a finite number of operations whether the equation is solvable in rational integers. The Entscheidungsproblem [decision problem for first-order logic ] is solved when we know a procedure that allows for any given logical expression to decide by finitely many operations its validity or satisfiability... The Entscheidungsproblem must be considered the main problem of mathematical logic.

— quoted, with this translation and the original German, in Dershowitz and Gurevich, 2008

By 1922 this notion of "Entscheidungsproblem" had developed a bit, and H. Behmann stated that

> ... most general form of the Entscheidungsproblem [is] as follows:

> A quite definite generally applicable prescription is required which will allow one to decide in a finite number of steps the truth or falsity of a given purely logical assertion...

— Gandy quoting Behmann

> Behmann remarks that... the general problem is equivalent to the problem of deciding which mathematical propositions are true.

— ibid.

> If one were able to solve the Entscheidungsproblem then one would have a "procedure for solving many (or even all) mathematical problems".

— ibid.

At the 1928 international congress of mathematicians, Hilbert "made his questions quite precise. First, was mathematics complete... Second, was mathematics consistent... And thirdly, was mathematics decidable ?" Kurt Gödel answered the first two questions in 1930, at the very same meeting where Hilbert gave his retirement speech (much to the chagrin of Hilbert). The third one, the Entscheidungsproblem, had to wait until the mid-1930s.

The problem was that to answer it you first needed a precise definition of "definite general applicable prescription", which the Princeton professor Alonzo Church would come to call "effective calculability", and in 1928 there was no such definition. Over the next 6–7 years Emil Post developed his definition, which was a worker moving from room to room writing and erasing marks per a list of instructions. Church and his two students Stephen Kleene and J. B. Rosser also developed one, by using Church's lambda-calculus and Gödel's recursion theory (1934). Church's paper was published 15 April 1936 and it showed that the Entscheidungsproblem was indeed "undecidable", and it beat Turing to the punch by almost a year (Turing's paper was submitted 28 May 1936 and published January 1937). Church refereed Turing's paper, and while he did, Turing had time to study Church's paper and add an Appendix where he sketched a proof that Church's lambda-calculus and his own machines would compute the same functions.

> But what Church had done was something rather different, and in a certain sense weaker.... the Turing construction was more direct, and provided an argument from first principles, closing the gap in Church's demonstration.

— Hodges

Post had only proposed a definition of calculability and criticised Church's "definition", but he had not proved anything.

## Historical background: computational machinery

Robin Gandy (1919–1995) was a student of Alan Turing (1912–1954), and also his lifelong friend. Gandy traces the idea of a "calculating machine" back to Charles Babbage (circa 1834), and he actually proposes something he calls "Babbage's Thesis":

> That the whole of development and operations of analysis are now capable of being executed by machinery.

— (italics in Babbage as cited by Gandy)

Gandy analyses Babbage's analytical engine and describes the following five operations that it has (cf. p. 52–53):

- The arithmetic functions +, −, ×, where − is "proper" subtraction: x − y = 0 if y ≥ x.
- Any sequence of operations is an operation.
- Iteration of an operation (repeating an operation P n times).
- Conditional iteration (repeating an operation P n times, conditional on the "success" of test T).
- Conditional transfer (i.e., a conditional "goto").

According to Gandy, "the functions which can be calculated by (1), (2), and (4) are precisely those which are Turing computable." He also cites other proposals for "universal calculating machines", which include the ones by Percy Ludgate (1909), Leonardo Torres Quevedo (1914), Maurice d'Ocagne (1922), Louis Couffignal (1933), Vannevar Bush (1936) and Howard Aiken (1937). But about these he says:

> … the emphasis is on programming a fixed iterable sequence of arithmetical operations. The fundamental importance of conditional iteration and conditional transfer for a general theory of calculating machines is not recognized…

— Gandy

## The Entscheidungsproblem (the "decision problem"): Hilbert's tenth question of 1900

The famous mathematician David Hilbert posed his problems in 1900, and one aspect of problem #10 had been floating around for almost 30 years before it got framed precisely. This is Hilbert's original expression for No. 10:

> 10. Determination of the solvability of a Diophantine equation. Given a Diophantine equation with any number of unknown quantities and with rational integral coefficients: To devise a process according to which it can be determined in a finite number of operations whether the equation is solvable in rational integers. The Entscheidungsproblem [decision problem for first-order logic ] is solved when we know a procedure that allows for any given logical expression to decide by finitely many operations its validity or satisfiability... The Entscheidungsproblem must be considered the main problem of mathematical logic.

— quoted, with this translation and the original German, in Dershowitz and Gurevich, 2008

By 1922 this notion of "Entscheidungsproblem" had developed a bit, and H. Behmann stated that

> ... most general form of the Entscheidungsproblem [is] as follows:

> A quite definite generally applicable prescription is required which will allow one to decide in a finite number of steps the truth or falsity of a given purely logical assertion...

— Gandy quoting Behmann

> Behmann remarks that... the general problem is equivalent to the problem of deciding which mathematical propositions are true.

— ibid.

> If one were able to solve the Entscheidungsproblem then one would have a "procedure for solving many (or even all) mathematical problems".

— ibid.

At the 1928 international congress of mathematicians, Hilbert "made his questions quite precise. First, was mathematics complete... Second, was mathematics consistent... And thirdly, was mathematics decidable ?" Kurt Gödel answered the first two questions in 1930, at the very same meeting where Hilbert gave his retirement speech (much to the chagrin of Hilbert). The third one, the Entscheidungsproblem, had to wait until the mid-1930s.

The problem was that to answer it you first needed a precise definition of "definite general applicable prescription", which the Princeton professor Alonzo Church would come to call "effective calculability", and in 1928 there was no such definition. Over the next 6–7 years Emil Post developed his definition, which was a worker moving from room to room writing and erasing marks per a list of instructions. Church and his two students Stephen Kleene and J. B. Rosser also developed one, by using Church's lambda-calculus and Gödel's recursion theory (1934). Church's paper was published 15 April 1936 and it showed that the Entscheidungsproblem was indeed "undecidable", and it beat Turing to the punch by almost a year (Turing's paper was submitted 28 May 1936 and published January 1937). Meanwhile Emil Post submitted a brief paper in the fall of 1936, so Turing at least had priority over Post. Church refereed Turing's paper, and while he did, Turing had time to study Church's paper and add an Appendix where he sketched a proof that Church's lambda-calculus and his own machines would compute the same functions.

> But what Church had done was something rather different, and in a certain sense weaker.... the Turing construction was more direct, and provided an argument from first principles, closing the gap in Church's demonstration.

— Hodges

Post had only proposed a definition of calculability and criticised Church's "definition", but he had not proved anything.

## Alan Turing's a-machine

In the spring of 1935 Turing, who was then a young Master's student at King's College, Cambridge, took on the challenge. He had been stimulated by the lectures of the logician M. H. A. Newman "and learned from them of Gödel's work and the Entscheidungsproblem... Newman used the word 'mechanical'...". In his obituary of Turing 1955 Newman writes:

> To the question 'what is a "mechanical" process?' Turing returned the characteristic answer 'Something that can be done by a machine' and he embarked on the highly congenial task of analysing the general notion of a computing machine.

— Gandy

Gandy also states that:

> I suppose, but do not know, that Turing, right from the start of his work, had as his goal a proof of the undecidability of the Entscheidungsproblem. He told me that the 'main idea' of the paper came to him when he was lying in Grantchester meadows in the summer of 1935. The 'main idea' might have either been his analysis of computation or his realization that there was a universal machine, and so a diagonal argument to prove unsolvability.

— ibid.

Gandy believed that Newman's statement above is "misleading", but not everyone shares this opinion. Turing had a lifelong interest in machines: "Alan had dreamt of inventing typewriters as a boy; [his mother] Mrs. Turing had a typewriter; and he could well have begun by asking himself what was meant by calling a typewriter 'mechanical'" (Hodges p. 96). When he was at Princeton doing his PhD, Turing built a Boolean-logic multiplier (see below). His PhD thesis is titled "Systems of Logic Based on Ordinals", and it contains this definition of "a computable function":

> It was stated above that 'a function is effectively calculable if its values can be found by some purely mechanical process'. We may take this statement literally, understanding by a purely mechanical process one which could be carried out by a machine. It is possible to give a mathematical description, in a certain normal form, of the structures of these machines. The development of these ideas leads to the author's definition of a computable function, and to an identification of computability with effective calculability. It is not difficult, though somewhat laborious, to prove that these three definitions [the 3rd is the λ-calculus] are equivalent.

— Turing (1939, p. 166)

Turing invented the "a-machine" (automatic machine) in 1936. He submitted his paper to the London Mathematical Society for its Proceedings on 31 May 1936, but it was published in early 1937, and offprints were available in February 1937. The term "Turing machine" was coined later by Turing's doctoral advisor, Alonzo Church, in a review. Using this model Turing could answer two questions in the negative:

- Does a machine exist that can determine whether any arbitrary machine on its tape is "circular" (e.g., freezes, or fails to continue its computational task)?
- Does a machine exist that can determine whether any arbitrary machine on its tape ever prints a given symbol?

So by giving a mathematical description of a very simple device that can do arbitrary computations, he was able to prove properties of computation in general, and in particular the uncomputability of the Entscheidungsproblem ('decision problem').

After Turing returned to the UK he ultimately became jointly responsible for breaking the German secret codes that were created by encryption machines called "The Enigma". He also got involved in the design of the ACE (Automatic Computing Engine): "[Turing's] ACE proposal was effectively self-contained, and its roots lay not in the EDVAC [the USA's initiative], but in his own universal machine" (Hodges p. 318). There are still arguments about the origin and nature of what Kleene (1952) named Turing's Thesis. But what Turing did prove with his computational-machine model is in his paper "On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem" (1937):

> [that] the Hilbert Entscheidungsproblem can have no solution... I propose, therefore to show that there can be no general process for determining whether a given formula U of the functional calculus K is provable, i.e. that there can be no machine which, supplied with any one U of these formulae, will eventually say whether U is provable.

— from Turing's paper as reprinted in The Undecidable, p. 145

Turing's example (his second proof) is this: if one asks for a general procedure to tell us "Does this machine ever print 0", the question is "undecidable".

## 1937–1970: The "digital computer", the birth of "computer science"

In 1937, while he was at Princeton working on his PhD thesis, Turing built a digital (Boolean-logic) multiplier from scratch, and he made his own electromechanical relays for it (Hodges p. 138). "Alan's task was to embody the logical design of a Turing machine in a network of relay-operated switches..." (Hodges p. 138). Turing might have just been curious and experimenting at first, but quite-earnest work in the same direction was going on in Germany by Konrad Zuse (1938) and in the United States by Howard Aiken and George Stibitz (1937). The fruits of their labors were used by both the Axis and the Allied militaries in World War II (cf. Hodges p. 298–299).

In the early to mid-1950s Hao Wang and Marvin Minsky reduced the Turing machine to a simpler form, which was a precursor to the Post–Turing machine of Martin Davis. At the same time European researchers were reducing the new-fangled electronic computer to a computer-like theoretical object that is equivalent to what is now being called a "Turing machine". In the late 1950s and early 1960s, the coincidentally parallel developments of Melzak and Lambek (1961), Minsky (1961), and Shepherdson and Sturgis (1961) took the European work further and reduced the Turing machine to a more friendly, computer-like abstract model which is called the counter machine. Elgot and Robinson (1964), Hartmanis (1971), and Cook and Reckhow (1973) took this work even further with the register machine and random-access machine models. But basically all of these are just multi-tape Turing machines with an arithmetic-like instruction set.

## 1970–present: as a model of computation

Today the counter, register and random-access machines, and also their sire the Turing machine, are still the models of choice for theorists who investigate questions in the theory of computation. In particular computational complexity theory uses the Turing machine:

> Depending on the objects one likes to manipulate in the computations (numbers like nonnegative integers or alphanumeric strings), two models have obtained a dominant position in machine-based complexity theory:

> the off-line multitape Turing machine..., which represents the standard model for string-oriented computation, and the random access machine (RAM) as introduced by Cook and Reckhow..., which models the idealised Von Neumann-style computer.

— Van Emde Boas (1990)

> Only in the related area of analysis of algorithms this role is taken over by the RAM model.

— Van Emde Boas (1990)
