## Historical background: computational machinery

Robin Gandy (1919–1995)—a student of Alan Turing (1912–1954), and his lifelong friend—traces the notion of "calculating machine" back to Charles Babbage (circa 1834) and proposes what he calls "Babbage's Thesis":

> That the whole of development and operations of analysis are now capable of being executed by machinery.

— (italics in Babbage as cited by Gandy)

Gandy's analysis of Babbage's analytical engine describes these five operations (cf. p. 52–53):

- The arithmetic functions +, −, ×, where − indicates "proper" subtraction: x − y = 0 if y ≥ x.

- Any sequence of operations is an operation.

- Iteration of an operation (repeating n times an operation P).

- Conditional iteration (repeating n times an operation P conditional on the "success" of test T).

- Conditional transfer (i.e., conditional " goto ").

Gandy states that "the functions which can be calculated by (1), (2), and (4) are precisely those which are Turing computable." He also cites other proposals for "universal calculating machines" including those of Percy Ludgate (1909), Leonardo Torres Quevedo (1914), Maurice d'Ocagne (1922), Louis Couffignal (1933), Vannevar Bush (1936) and Howard Aiken (1937). However:

> … the emphasis is on programming a fixed iterable sequence of arithmetical operations. The fundamental importance of conditional iteration and conditional transfer for a general theory of calculating machines is not recognized…

— Gandy

## The Entscheidungsproblem (the "decision problem"): Hilbert's tenth question of 1900

Of the problems posed by the famous mathematician David Hilbert in 1900, an aspect of problem #10 had been floating around for almost 30 years before it was framed precisely. Hilbert's original expression for No. 10 is as follows:

> 10. Determination of the solvability of a Diophantine equation. Given a Diophantine equation with any number of unknown quantities and with rational integral coefficients: To devise a process according to which it can be determined in a finite number of operations whether the equation is solvable in rational integers. The Entscheidungsproblem [decision problem for first-order logic ] is solved when we know a procedure that allows for any given logical expression to decide by finitely many operations its validity or satisfiability... The Entscheidungsproblem must be considered the main problem of mathematical logic.

— quoted, with this translation and the original German, in Dershowitz and Gurevich, 2008

By 1922, this notion of " Entscheidungsproblem " had developed somewhat, and H. Behmann stated that

> ... most general form of the Entscheidungsproblem [is] as follows:

> A quite definite generally applicable prescription is required which will allow one to decide in a finite number of steps the truth or falsity of a given purely logical assertion...

— Gandy quoting Behmann

> Behmann remarks that... the general problem is equivalent to the problem of deciding which mathematical propositions are true.

— ibid.

> If one were able to solve the Entscheidungsproblem then one would have a "procedure for solving many (or even all) mathematical problems".

— ibid.

At the 1928 international congress of mathematicians, Hilbert "made his questions quite precise. First, was mathematics complete... Second, was mathematics consistent... And thirdly, was mathematics decidable ?" The first two questions were answered in 1930 by Kurt Gödel at the very same meeting where Hilbert delivered his retirement speech (much to the chagrin of Hilbert); the third—the Entscheidungsproblem —had to wait until the mid-1930s.

The problem was that answering it first required a precise definition of "definite general applicable prescription", which Princeton professor Alonzo Church would come to call " effective calculability ", and in 1928 no such definition existed. Over the next 6–7 years Emil Post developed his definition of a worker moving from room to room writing and erasing marks per a list of instructions, as did Church and his two students Stephen Kleene and J. B. Rosser by use of Church's lambda-calculus and Gödel's recursion theory (1934). Church's paper (published 15 April 1936) showed that the Entscheidungsproblem was indeed "undecidable" [1] and beat Turing to the punch by almost a year (Turing's paper submitted 28 May 1936, published January 1937). Meanwhile, Emil Post submitted a brief paper in the fall of 1936, so Turing at least had priority over Post. While Church refereed Turing's paper, Turing had time to study Church's paper and add an Appendix where he sketched a proof that Church's lambda-calculus and his machines would compute the same functions.

> But what Church had done was something rather different, and in a certain sense weaker.... the Turing construction was more direct, and provided an argument from first principles, closing the gap in Church's demonstration.

— Hodges

Post had only proposed a definition of calculability and criticised Church's "definition", but had not proved anything.

## Alan Turing's a-machine

In the spring of 1935, Turing as a young Master's student at King's College, Cambridge, took on the challenge; he had been stimulated by the lectures of the logician M. H. A. Newman "and learned from them of Gödel's work and the Entscheidungsproblem... Newman used the word 'mechanical'... In his obituary of Turing 1955 Newman writes:

Turing had a lifelong interest in machines: "Alan had dreamt of inventing typewriters as a boy; [his mother] Mrs. Turing had a typewriter; and he could well have begun by asking himself what was meant by calling a typewriter 'mechanical'" (Hodges p. 96). While he was at Princeton pursuing his PhD, Turing built a Boolean-logic multiplier (see below). We may take this statement literally, understanding by a purely mechanical process one which could be carried out by a machine. The development of these ideas leads to the author's definition of a computable function, and to an identification of computability with effective calculability. steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Intro
  - Church: proof of undecidability of a problem in lambda calculus, April 1936
  - Turing's proof later, January 1937
  - many other undecidable problems since; halting problem emerged in 1950s
## Timeline
- 1900: Hilbert, "23 questions" (Hilbert's problems), Second International Congress of Mathematicians, Paris
  - [quote: the second problem = consistency of Peano axioms]
- 1920–1921: Emil Post, halting problem for tag systems, candidate for unsolvability
  - unsolvability established much later, by Marvin Minsky
- 1928: Hilbert recasts 'Second Problem', Bologna International Congress
  - three questions: complete? consistent? decidable?
  - third = Entscheidungsproblem (Decision Problem)
- 1930: Gödel announces proof answering first two of the 1928 questions
  - [quote: Hilbert's reaction; Gödel didn't think it contradicted Hilbert's formalism]
- 1931: Gödel publishes "On Formally Undecidable Propositions of Principia Mathematica and Related Systems I"
- 19 April 1935: Church, "An Unsolvable Problem of Elementary Number Theory"
  - effectively calculable = general recursive functions = lambda-definable functions
  - halting problem for lambda calculus (does a lambda-expression have a normal form) not effectively calculable
- 1936: Church, first proof Entscheidungsproblem unsolvable, via recursive functions
- 7 October 1936: Post's "Finite Combinatory Processes. Formulation I" received
  - instruction "(C) Stop"; [quote: "type 1" process]
- May 1936 – January 1937: Turing, On Computable Numbers With an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem
  - to press May 1936, in print January 1937
  - three problems undecidable: "satisfaction", "printing", Entscheidungsproblem
  - differs from Church: computation by machine
  - one of the "first examples of decision problems proved unsolvable"
- 1939: J. Barkley Rosser, essential equivalence of "effective method" (Gödel, Church, Turing)
- 1943: Kleene paper, [quote: procedure that necessarily terminates, 'Yes' or 'No']
- 1952: Kleene, halting problem for Turing machines, machines that "eventually stop"
  - [quote: Kleene 1952]
- 1952: Martin Davis uses 'halting problem' in lectures, Control Systems Laboratory, University of Illinois
  - likely first use of the term
## Origin of the halting problem
- papers/textbooks credit Turing's 1936 paper -> not correct
  - Turing never used "halt"/"halting" in published works
- literature search 1936–1958: first published use = Rogers (1957)
  - but Rogers had draft of Davis (1958); Davis intro [quote: "some novelty in the arrangement"]
  - so terminology attributed to Davis; letter: using it since 1952
- [quote: Davis's book, definition + Theorem 2.2 + printing problem]
- precursor: Kleene 1952, differs only in wording [quote]
- halting problem Turing equivalent to Davis's printing problem and Turing's 1936 printing problem
  - Turing equivalence loose; machines print but don't halt, halt but don't print
  - different issues, conceptual and technical differences
  - Davis being modest [quote: Davis on Turing]

In April 1936 Alonzo Church published a proof that a problem in the lambda calculus was undecidable. Turing's proof came later, in January 1937. Since then many other undecidable problems have been described, and the halting problem is one of them; it emerged in the 1950s.

## Timeline

- 1900: David Hilbert poses his "23 questions", which are now known as Hilbert's problems, at the Second International Congress of Mathematicians in Paris. [quote: the second problem was proving the consistency of the Peano axioms]

- 1920–1921: Emil Post looks at the halting problem for tag systems and thinks it is a candidate for unsolvability. It was not shown to be unsolvable until much later, by Marvin Minsky.

- 1928: At the Bologna International Congress Hilbert recasts his 'Second Problem'. He posed three questions: #1 was mathematics complete, #2 was mathematics consistent, #3 was mathematics decidable. The third question is the Entscheidungsproblem (Decision Problem).

steps.text:
In April 1936 Alonzo Church published a proof that a problem in the lambda calculus was undecidable. Turing's proof was published later than that, in January 1937. Since then a lot of other undecidable problems have been described, and one of them is the halting problem, which emerged in the 1950s.

## Timeline

- 1900: David Hilbert poses his "23 questions" at the Second International Congress of Mathematicians in Paris. These are now known as Hilbert's problems. "Of these, the second was that of proving the consistency of the ' Peano axioms ' on which, as he had shown, the rigour of mathematics depended".

- 1920–1921: Emil Post looks at the halting problem for tag systems and he regards it as a candidate for unsolvability. Its unsolvability was not established until much later, and it was Marvin Minsky who did it.

- 1928: Hilbert recasts his 'Second Problem' at the Bologna International Congress. He posed three questions, which were: #1: Was mathematics complete? #2: Was mathematics consistent? #3: Was mathematics decidable? The third question is the one that is known as the Entscheidungsproblem (Decision Problem).

- 1930: Kurt Gödel announces a proof which answers the first two of Hilbert's 1928 questions. "At first he [Hilbert] was only angry and frustrated, but then he began to try to deal constructively with the problem... Gödel himself felt—and expressed the thought in his paper—that his work did not contradict Hilbert's formalistic point of view".

- 1931: Gödel publishes "On Formally Undecidable Propositions of Principia Mathematica and Related Systems I".

- 19 April 1935: Alonzo Church publishes "An Unsolvable Problem of Elementary Number Theory". The paper proposes that the intuitive notion of an effectively calculable function can be formalized by the general recursive functions, or equivalently by the lambda-definable functions. He proves that the halting problem for lambda calculus is not effectively calculable, i.e. whether a given lambda-expression has a normal form.

- 1936: Church publishes the first proof that the Entscheidungsproblem is unsolvable, and he uses a notion of calculation by recursive functions to do it.

- 7 October 1936: Emil Post's paper "Finite Combinatory Processes. Formulation I" is received. Post adds an instruction "(C) Stop" to his "process". He called such a process "type 1... if the process it determines terminates for each specific problem."

- May 1936 – January 1937: Alan Turing's paper On Computable Numbers With an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem goes to press in May 1936 and it reaches print in January 1937. In the paper Turing proves three problems undecidable, which are the "satisfaction" problem, the "printing" problem, and the Entscheidungsproblem. The difference between Turing's proof and Church's proof is that Turing introduces the notion of computation by machine. This is one of the "first examples of decision problems proved unsolvable".

- 1939: J. Barkley Rosser observes that the "effective method" defined by Gödel, Church, and Turing are essentially equivalent.

- 1943: Stephen Kleene states in a paper that "In setting up a complete algorithmic theory, what we do is describe a procedure... which procedure necessarily terminates and in such manner that from the outcome we can read a definite answer, 'Yes' or 'No,' to the question, 'Is the predicate value true?'."

- 1952: Kleene includes a discussion of the unsolvability of the halting problem for Turing machines. He reformulates it in terms of machines that "eventually stop", i.e. halt: "...there is no algorithm for deciding whether any given machine, when started from any given situation, eventually stops."

- 1952: Martin Davis uses the term 'halting problem' in a series of lectures at the Control Systems Laboratory at the University of Illinois in 1952. This is likely the first such use of the term.

## Origin of the halting problem

Many papers and textbooks say that the definition and proof of undecidability of the halting problem is in Turing's 1936 paper. But this is not correct. Turing did not use the terms "halt" or "halting" in any of his published works, and this includes his 1936 paper. If you search the academic literature from 1936 to 1958, the first published material that uses the term "halting problem" is Rogers (1957). However, Rogers says that he had a draft of Davis (1958) available to him, and in the introduction Martin Davis states that "the expert will perhaps find some novelty in the arrangement and treatment of topics", so the terminology must be attributed to Davis. Davis stated in a letter that he had been referring to the halting problem since 1952. This is how Davis's book uses it:

> "[...] we wish to determine whether or not [a Turing machine] Z, if placed in a given initial state, will eventually halt. We call this problem the halting problem for Z. [...]

> Theorem 2.2 There exists a Turing machine whose halting problem is recursively unsolvable.

> A related problem is the printing problem for a simple Turing machine Z with respect to a symbol S i ".

Kleene's 1952 statement is a possible precursor to Davis's formulation, and it only differs in wording:

> there is no algorithm for deciding whether any given machine, when started from any given situation, eventually stops.

The halting problem is Turing equivalent to Davis's printing problem ("does a Turing machine starting from a given state ever print a given symbol?"), and it is also Turing equivalent to the printing problem in Turing's 1936 paper ("does a Turing machine starting from a blank tape ever print a given symbol?"). But Turing equivalence is rather loose and it does not mean the two problems are the same. Some machines print but do not halt, and some halt but do not print. The printing problem and the halting problem address different issues and they have important conceptual and technical differences. So Davis was just being modest when he said:

> It might also be mentioned that the unsolvability of essentially these problems was first obtained by Turing.

However, Turing equivalence is rather loose and does not mean that the two problems are the same. There are machines which print but do not halt, and halt but not print. The printing and halting problems address different issues and exhibit important conceptual and technical differences. Thus, Davis was simply being modest when he said:

> It might also be mentioned that the unsolvability of essentially these problems was first obtained by Turing.

[8] Textual search of Turing's collected works: Good (1992), Gandy & Yates (2001), Ince (1992), Saunders (1992). Similarly Hodges (1983) does not have the word "halting" or words "halting problem" in his index.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Tony Hoare developed the quicksort algorithm in 1959, when he was a visiting student at Moscow State University. Hoare was at that time working on a machine translation project for the National Physical Laboratory. As part of the translation process he needed to sort the words in Russian sentences before he looked them up in a Russian-English dictionary, which was on magnetic tape in alphabetical order. His first idea was insertion sort, but he recognized that it would be slow, so he came up with a new idea. He wrote the partition part in Mercury Autocode, but he had trouble dealing with the list of unsorted segments. When he returned to England he was asked to write code for Shellsort. Hoare told his boss that he knew of a faster algorithm and his boss bet a sixpence that he did not. In the end his boss accepted that he lost the bet. Hoare published a paper about his algorithm, which included a theoretical analysis, in The Computer Journal Volume 5, Issue 1, 1962, Pages 10–16. Later Hoare learned about ALGOL and that it was able to do recursion, and this enabled him to publish an improved version of the algorithm in ALGOL in Communications of the Association for Computing Machinery, which was the premier computer science journal at the time. The ALGOL code was published in Communications of the ACM (CACM), Volume 4, Issue 7 July 1961, pp 321 Algorithm 63: partition and Algorithm 64: Quicksort.

Quicksort was widely adopted, for example it appeared in Unix as the default library sort subroutine. So it lent its name to the C standard library subroutine qsort and it was also in the reference implementation of Java.

Robert Sedgewick's PhD thesis in 1975 is considered a milestone in the study of Quicksort. In it he resolved many open problems about the analysis of various pivot selection schemes, including Samplesort and adaptive partitioning by Van Emden, and he also derived the expected number of comparisons and swaps. In 1993 Jon Bentley and Doug McIlroy incorporated various improvements for use in programming libraries. These included a technique for dealing with equal elements and a pivot scheme that is called pseudomedian of nine, where a sample of nine elements is split into groups of three and then the median of the three medians from the three groups is chosen. In his book Programming Pearls, Bentley described another partitioning scheme that was simpler and compact, and he attributed it to Nico Lomuto. Bentley later wrote that he used Hoare's version for years but never really understood it, but Lomuto's version was simple enough to prove correct. In the same essay Bentley described Quicksort as the "most beautiful code I had ever written". Lomuto's partition scheme was also popularized by the textbook Introduction to Algorithms, though it is inferior to Hoare's scheme because on average it does three times more swaps and it degrades to O (n 2) runtime when all elements are equal. In 1998 McIlroy would further produce an AntiQuicksort (aqsort) function, which produces adversarial data on-the-fly and consistently drives even his 1993 variant of Quicksort into quadratic behavior.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- What a hash function does in a table; perfect hash functions
## Integer universe assumption (which schemes are used)
## Hashing by division
## Hashing by multiplication
## String hashing
## Choosing a hash function (uniformity, runs, K-independence)

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- hash function h:U\rightarrow \{0,...,m-1\}: universe U of keys -> indices / slots of the table; h(x)\in \{0,...,m-1\} for x\in U
- conventional implementations: integer universe assumption — all elements from U=\{0,...,u-1\}, bit length of u within word size of the computer architecture
- perfect hash function for a set S: injective on S (each x\in S to a different value in {0,...,m-1})
- perfect hash possible if all keys known ahead of time

## Integer universe assumption
- schemes: hashing by division, by multiplication, universal hashing, dynamic perfect hashing, static perfect hashing
- division = the commonly used one

## Hashing by division
- h(x)\ =\ x\,{\bmod {\,}}m; h(x) = hash value of x\in S, m = table size

## Hashing by multiplication
- h(x)=\lfloor m{\bigl (}(xA){\bmod {1}}{\bigr)}\rfloor; A non-integer real-valued constant, m table size
- advantage: m not critical
- any A works; Donald Knuth suggests golden ratio

## String hashing
- strings commonly used as keys
- The C++ Programming Language (3rd ed.): unsigned int starting at zero, left shift one bit, xor with integer value of next character; result modulo table size
- non-circular shift: string length at least eight bits less than size of the unsigned int in bits
- alternative: polynomial rolling hash function

## Choosing a hash function
- uniform distribution of hash values = fundamental requirement
- non-uniform -> more collisions, higher cost of resolving them
- hard to ensure by design; evaluate empirically with statistical tests, e.g. Pearson's chi-squared test for discrete uniform distributions
- uniformity only needed for table sizes that occur in the application
  - dynamic resizing, exact doubling/halving -> only power-of-two sizes; index = range of bits of the hash
  - some hashing algorithms prefer prime sizes
- open addressing: avoid runs (two or more keys -> consecutive slots); lookup cost can skyrocket even with low load factor and infrequent collisions
- popular multiplicative hash claimed to have particularly poor run behavior
- K-independent hashing: prove no bad keysets for a given type of hashtable
  - results known for linear probing, cuckoo hashing
  - then focus on fastest such function

steps.text:
A hash function h:U\rightarrow \{0,...,m-1\} maps the universe U of keys to indices or slots in the table, which means h(x)\in \{0,...,m-1\} for x\in U. Conventional implementations of hash functions are based on the integer universe assumption, which is that all the elements of the table come from the universe U=\{0,...,u-1\}, where the bit length of u is confined within the word size of a computer architecture.

A hash function h is called perfect for a given set S if it is injective on S, which means that each element x\in S maps to a different value in {0,...,m-1}. If all of the keys are known ahead of time, a perfect hash function can be created.

## Integer universe assumption

There are several hashing schemes that are used under the integer universe assumption: hashing by division, hashing by multiplication, universal hashing, dynamic perfect hashing, and static perfect hashing. But hashing by division is the scheme that is commonly used.

## Hashing by division

In hashing by division the scheme is: h(x)\ =\ x\,{\bmod {\,}}m, where h(x) is the hash value of x\in S and m is the size of the table.

## Hashing by multiplication

In hashing by multiplication the scheme is: h(x)=\lfloor m{\bigl (}(xA){\bmod {1}}{\bigr)}\rfloor where A is a non-integer real-valued constant and m is the size of the table. One advantage of hashing by multiplication is that m is not critical. Any value A produces a hash function, but Donald Knuth suggests using the golden ratio.

## String hashing
- strings commonly used as keys
- The C++ Programming Language (3rd ed.): unsigned int starting at zero, left shift one bit, xor with integer value of next character; result modulo table size
- non-circular shift: string length at least eight bits less than size of the unsigned int in bits
- alternative: polynomial rolling hash function

## Choosing a hash function
- uniform distribution of hash values = fundamental requirement
- non-uniform -> more collisions, higher cost of resolving them
- hard to ensure by design; evaluate empirically with statistical tests, e.g. Pearson's chi-squared test for discrete uniform distributions
- uniformity only needed for table sizes that occur in the application

  - some hashing algorithms prefer prime sizes

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
A hash function h:U\rightarrow \{0,...,m-1\} maps the universe U of keys to indices or slots in the table, which means h(x)\in \{0,...,m-1\} for x\in U. Conventional implementations of hash functions are based on the integer universe assumption, which is that all the elements of the table come from the universe U=\{0,...,u-1\}, where the bit length of u is confined within the word size of a computer architecture.

A hash function h is called perfect for a given set S if it is injective on S, which means that each element x\in S maps to a different value in {0,...,m-1}. If all of the keys are known ahead of time, a perfect hash function can be created.

## Integer universe assumption

There are several hashing schemes that are used under the integer universe assumption: hashing by division, hashing by multiplication, universal hashing, dynamic perfect hashing, and static perfect hashing. But hashing by division is the scheme that is commonly used.

## Hashing by division

In hashing by division the scheme is: h(x)\ =\ x\,{\bmod {\,}}m, where h(x) is the hash value of x\in S and m is the size of the table.

## Hashing by multiplication

In hashing by multiplication the scheme is: h(x)=\lfloor m{\bigl (}(xA){\bmod {1}}{\bigr)}\rfloor where A is a non-integer real-valued constant and m is the size of the table. One advantage of hashing by multiplication is that m is not critical. Any value A produces a hash function, but Donald Knuth suggests using the golden ratio.

## String hashing

A string is commonly used as the key to the hash function. The third edition of The C++ Programming Language describes a simple hash function where an unsigned integer that starts at zero is repeatedly left shifted one bit and then xor'ed with the integer value of the next character, and then this hash value is taken modulo the table size. If the left shift is not circular, the string length should be at least eight bits less than the size of the unsigned integer in bits. A polynomial rolling hash function is another common way to hash a string to an integer.

## Choosing a hash function

A fundamental requirement of a hash function is uniform distribution of the hash values. If the distribution is not uniform, the number of collisions goes up and so does the cost of resolving them. It is sometimes hard to ensure uniformity by design, but it can be evaluated empirically with statistical tests, e.g., a Pearson's chi-squared test for discrete uniform distributions.

The distribution only has to be uniform for the table sizes that occur in the application. In particular, if dynamic resizing is used with exact doubling and halving of the table size, then the hash function only needs to be uniform when the size is a power of two. In that case the index can be computed as some range of bits of the hash function. On the other hand some hashing algorithms prefer the size to be a prime number.

For open addressing schemes the hash function should also avoid runs, which is the mapping of two or more keys to consecutive slots. Runs like this may cause the lookup cost to skyrocket, even when the load factor is low and collisions are infrequent. The popular multiplicative hash is claimed to have particularly poor run behavior.

K-independent hashing gives a way to prove that a certain hash function does not have bad keysets for a given type of hashtable. A number of K-independence results are known for collision resolution schemes like linear probing and cuckoo hashing. Since K-independence can prove that a hash function works, one can then focus on finding the fastest possible such hash function.

steps.text:
Alonzo Church introduced the lambda calculus in the 1930s, as part of his investigation into the foundations of mathematics. In 1935 the original system was shown to be logically inconsistent, when Stephen Kleene and J. B. Rosser developed the Kleene–Rosser paradox.

After that, in 1936 Church isolated just the part that was relevant to computation and published it; this is what is now called the untyped lambda calculus. In 1940 he also introduced a system that was computationally weaker but logically consistent, the simply typed lambda calculus.

The lambda calculus was only a formalism until the 1960s, when its relation to programming languages was clarified. Because of Richard Montague and other linguists who applied it to the semantics of natural language, it has started to have a respectable place in both linguistics and computer science.

## Origin of the λ symbol
- uncertain why Church chose Greek letter lambda (\lambda) for function-abstraction; partly Church's own conflicting explanations
- Cardone and Hindley (2006) [quote: letter to Harald Dickson; {\hat {x}} -> \land x -> \lambda; Rosser 1984; later "more accidental"]
- Dana Scott, various public lectures: asked John W. Addison Jr., Church's former student and son-in-law
- Addison's postcard to Church [quote: iota/epsilon, why lambda?]
- Church's reply: returned postcard with "eeny, meeny, miny, moe"

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The lambda calculus was introduced by the mathematician Alonzo Church in the 1930s, as part of an investigation he was doing into the foundations of mathematics. The original system turned out to be logically inconsistent, which was shown in 1935 when Stephen Kleene and J. B. Rosser developed the Kleene–Rosser paradox.

After this, in 1936 Church isolated the portion that was relevant to computation and published just that, and this is what is now called the untyped lambda calculus. In 1940 he also introduced a system that was computationally weaker, but logically consistent, which is known as the simply typed lambda calculus.

Up until the 1960s, when its relation to programming languages was clarified, the lambda calculus was only a formalism. Richard Montague and other linguists applied it in the semantics of natural language, and thanks to this the lambda calculus has begun to enjoy a respectable place in both linguistics and computer science.

## Origin of the λ symbol

It is somewhat uncertain why Church used the Greek letter lambda (\lambda) as the notation for function-abstraction in the lambda calculus, and part of the reason may be that Church himself gave conflicting explanations. Cardone and Hindley (2006) write:

> By the way, why did Church choose the notation " \lambda "? In [an unpublished 1964 letter to Harald Dickson] he stated clearly that it came from the notation " {\hat {x}} " used for class-abstraction by Whitehead and Russell, by first modifying " {\hat {x}} " to " \land x " to distinguish function-abstraction from class-abstraction, and then changing " \land " to " \lambda " for ease of printing.

> This origin was also reported in [Rosser, 1984, p.338]. On the other hand, in his later years Church told two enquirers that the choice was more accidental: a symbol was needed and \lambda just happened to be chosen.

Dana Scott has also talked about this question in various public lectures. Scott tells the story that he once asked Church's former student and son-in-law John W. Addison Jr. a question about where the lambda symbol came from, and Addison then wrote his father-in-law a postcard:

> Dear Professor Church,

> Russell had the iota operator, Hilbert had the epsilon operator. Why did you choose lambda for your operator?

Scott says that Church's whole response was to return the postcard with the following annotation: " eeny, meeny, miny, moe ".
